# Building Innovation Capacity Across a Multinational Footprint
### Recommendation to the Executive Committee — for review with country leadership before release

**Stated assumptions** (to be corrected in week 1, before anything is announced): ~6,000–10,000 employees; 12–18 countries; established core business; group revenue in the €1.5–2.5bn range. All figures below scale with these numbers. Confidence in the structural recommendations (Moves 1–3, funding mechanics, legal sequencing) is high; confidence in site-level design choices is deliberately low until the diagnostic is complete, and those choices are left to local leadership.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

**Diagnosis.** The variance between locations is not a variance in creative capability; it is a variance in local mandate, decision latency, and remembered consequence. Branches with no real domain ownership, long approval chains, and a visible example of an unrewarded attempt behave exactly as rational people should. Middle management is the binding layer: managers are currently measured on predictability while being asked to sponsor variance.

**The three moves for the first 90 days** (everything else in this paper is downstream of these):

| # | Move | Why first |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Transfer two genuine domain mandates to two named branches**, with P&L and headcount attached | Changes structural incentive, not atmosphere. Highest leverage on location variance. |
| **2** | **Publish group-wide decision rights and reversible/irreversible thresholds**, with a decision-latency clock | The only intervention that reaches every site at once and closes the equity gap created by piloting. |
| **3** | **Change the manager scorecard** (with an anti-gaming quality gate), beginning works-council consultation in week 1 | Without this, Moves 1 and 2 are absorbed and neutralised at the middle layer. |

**Year-1 cost envelope: €9–14m**, of which €6–8m is a ring-fenced off-cycle experimentation fund (recoverable as portfolio investment, not overhead), €2.2m sized slack time in designated roles, €0.8m platform and translation capacity, €0.4m diagnostic, and ~€1.5m rotation and exchange.

**Expected outcomes by month 24:** competitive-response time-to-market reduced from baseline (to be measured; typically 24–30 weeks in companies of this profile) to ≤10 weeks; idea-to-first-cheap-test from ~90 days to ≤21 days; share of newly adopted group initiatives originating outside HQ rising from baseline to ≥35%.

**The two biggest risks.** (i) *Relational risk:* mandate transfer and manager re-scoring will be read at HQ and by some country heads as a loss of standing. If this is announced before individual pre-alignment with each affected leader, resistance will be quiet, indefinite, and very difficult to name. (ii) *Structural risk:* the annual budget cycle. If experimentation money is not ring-fenced off-cycle, staged funding cannot function and the programme dies at the second budget review.

---

## 2. Summary Table

| Intervention | Accountable owner | Year-1 cost | Time to effect | Primary metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mandate transfer to 2 branches | COO (Exec Sponsor: CEO) | Cost-neutral (reallocation) | 6–12 months | Share of adopted initiatives originating outside HQ |
| Decision rights + reversible/irreversible thresholds | Group General Counsel + COO | <€0.2m | 60–90 days | % decisions closed without escalation; approval-step count |
| Manager scorecard change | CHRO | <€0.3m (+ consultation time) | 6–9 months (IR-dependent) | Bet-quality review score; ideas advanced beyond manager's remit |
| Ring-fenced experimentation fund | CFO | €6–8m | 90 days to open | Idea-to-first-test days; portfolio kill rate |
| Market-signal capture and latency clock | Chief Strategy / Commercial Officer | €0.5m | 3–6 months | Signal-to-decision days |
| Sized slack (designated roles only) | Site heads | €2.2m | 6 months | Experiments started *and* stopped |
| Voice design + language capacity | CHRO + site heads | €0.8m | 3–9 months | Repeat contributor ratio; within-site safety trend |
| Rotation and cross-border pairing | CHRO | €1.5m | 12–18 months | Cross-site initiatives; norm transfer (qualitative) |
| Legal/IR enablement (invention remuneration, GDPR, councils) | GC + CHRO | €0.4m | Prerequisite | Countries cleared to launch |

---

## 3. Diagnostic First — The Instrument (Weeks 1–6)

Run this per site, through the site's own leadership rather than around it, and in the local language. Local leaders should see their site's results before the centre discusses them; this preserves standing and produces honest data.

Four questions to each of ~15 people per site, plus documented process trace:

1. **What happened to the last three ideas you had?** (Trace each: raised / absorbed / declined / never voiced — and to whom.)
2. **How many people must say yes before something small can be tried, and how long does that take in calendar days?** (Verify against actual records.)
3. **What do people here believe happens to someone who tries something and it does not work?** (Ask about "people here," not the respondent — this reduces exposure and yields better data in higher power-distance and higher uncertainty-avoidance settings.)
4. **Whose career here was visibly helped by an idea that did not work?** (Name or blank. A blank answer is the finding.)

Plus: which locations are *already* innovating in ways the centre has not noticed? Ask customers and country finance, not only management.

The variance in the answers is the actual map. Two hypotheses must be separated before treating anything: **ideas exist but stay unvoiced** (a safety and channel problem) versus **ideas are not being formed** (a mandate and market-exposure problem). These require different remedies.

---

## 4. Move 1 — Redistribute Real Mandates (Lead Lever)

Subsidiary initiative rises with the substance of local charter, not with encouragement (Birkinshaw's work on subsidiary initiative is directly on point; we treat this as well-supported).

**Selection criteria for the first two mandates:**
- Genuine local advantage: proximity to a fast-moving, price-sensitive, or regulation-leading market
- Existing initiative signal from the diagnostic (a site already improvising)
- A customer segment or product line where central standards are demonstrably a poor fit
- Site leadership willing to accept accountability, confirmed privately in advance

**What "mandate" must include, or it will not be believed:** P&L ownership for the domain; headcount authority; product roadmap authority for that domain including the right to diverge from group standards with documented reasoning; a seat at the group product forum; and a defined multi-year horizon so the site is not judged on quarter three.

**Reverse flow, made visible.** When a practice originating in a non-HQ site is adopted group-wide, the announcement names the originating site and its people. One such adoption is worth more than a year of messaging. Handle the mirror case with care: adopting from a branch should never be framed as HQ having been wrong, which costs face at the centre and slows the second adoption.

**Pre-alignment is not optional.** Before any announcement: individual conversations with the HQ function heads who will lose scope, with the two receiving site heads, and with the country heads not selected — including a stated pathway for the next round. Consensus built quietly in advance is what makes the public step uncontroversial.

---

## 5. Move 2 — Decision Rights, Thresholds, and Latency (One Consolidated Change)

This is the universal floor: it goes to every site on day one, including — especially — the quiet ones.

- **Publish, in plain language and every working language, what each level can decide alone.** Ambiguity in authority defaults to caution: where people cannot tell whether permission is needed, they assume it is.
- **Classify decisions reversible vs. irreversible.** Reversible: decided locally, fast, no committee. Irreversible or reputation-bearing: full scrutiny and senior involvement. Most established companies apply irreversible-decision governance to reversible decisions; that single misclassification explains much of the observed inertia.
- **Cap approval steps** for reversible spend below threshold at one.
- **Set a decision-latency target and measure it**: signal-to-decision ≤10 working days for reversible market responses; funded experiment start ≤21 days from submission.
- **Discretionary spend authority set as a percentage, not a currency figure.** Recommendation: a team lead may commit up to **2% of their team's annual cost base per quarter** without a business case, floored at a locally meaningful minimum and reviewed against local PPP. A flat "few thousand euros" grants a Zurich lead trivial latitude and a Manila lead unusual latitude — and re-creates the centre–periphery inequality we are trying to dissolve.
- **Procurement and legal fast lane.** A pre-approved vendor list, standard short-form contract, and 5-working-day SLA for experiment-scale purchases below threshold. Standard cycles of 6–12 weeks make "cheap test" impossible regardless of culture.

---

## 6. Move 3 — The Middle Layer

Asking managers to sponsor variance while grading them on variance suppression asks them to accept a personal cost. Correct the scorecard, and protect their standing while doing it.

**Add to manager evaluation (weighted ~15–20%):**
- **Bet quality, peer-reviewed** — not experiment count. A quarterly portfolio review by a small cross-site panel scores the manager's supported experiments on hypothesis clarity, proportionality of cost, and promptness of stopping. This replaces the gameable count; raw counts are retained as a diagnostic indicator only, explicitly unscored.
- **Ideas advanced beyond the manager's own remit** — sponsoring someone else's idea into another unit earns visible credit.
- **Decisions delegated** and permission requests eliminated.

**Cover, given publicly and specifically.** A manager who backs a well-run experiment that fails must be seen being supported by their own superior, in the same forum where the failure became visible. This is the single cheapest and most decisive signal available.

**One teachable skill, coached at scale.** The reflexive first response to an unpolished idea — "have you considered the cost?" — is the moment innovation usually stops. The substitute: "what would you need to test this cheaply?" Small, teachable, high-leverage.

**Consultation before announcement.** In Germany, the Netherlands, France, Austria and the Nordics, changes to evaluation criteria, reward schemes, working-time allocation, and any participation monitoring frequently fall under works-council consultation or co-determination. Begin in week 1. Treated as a partnership, councils shorten adoption; treated as an obstacle, they extend it by two or three quarters. Sequence country launches accordingly and do not pretend to a uniform go-live date.

---

## 7. Market Responsiveness — The Latency Workstream

Creativity and responsiveness are different problems. Responsiveness is latency.

- **Front-line signal capture.** Every customer-facing role gets a 60-second structured channel for one thing: "what I heard that we cannot currently serve." Local language, mobile, no form. Weekly triage at site level, not at HQ.
- **Named signal owners per market.** One accountable person per country compiles a monthly two-page market delta: competitor moves, regulatory shifts, lost-deal reasons, and price signals. Sites nearest fast-moving markets are treated as sensors, not as noise.
- **A single latency clock, published.** Signal received → decision → shipped change. Publish the median and the worst case monthly by region. Visibility of the clock does more than any exhortation.
- **A standing weekly response forum** with pre-delegated authority to commit up to a defined threshold. Decisions in the forum, not after it.
- **Divergence from central standards read as signal.** Where a site has quietly worked around a group process to serve its market, the default question is what the workaround reveals, not who authorised it.

Target state: front-line insight in Kuala Lumpur to shipped change in eight weeks for reversible product or pricing responses, with the site deciding, not requesting.

---

## 8. Strategic Focus and Portfolio Logic

Without focus, a low-threshold pipeline produces high volume and low strategic value.

- **Four to six named strategic challenge questions**, set by the Executive Committee, refreshed annually, phrased as problems not solutions — e.g. "how do we serve SMEs profitably in low-ARPU markets?"; "where does regulation in Market X become an advantage?" Ideas outside these areas remain welcome but are funded from a smaller pool.
- **Portfolio allocation:** 70% core improvement / 20% adjacent / 10% new-to-company, allocated at group level and reviewed quarterly. Sites hold their own sub-portfolios.
- **Explicit kill criteria set at funding, not at review.** Every funded experiment states in advance what result would stop it and by when. Stopping on pre-agreed criteria is recorded as successful execution — this removes the personal cost of stopping and protects the sponsor's standing.
- **Ring-fenced, off-cycle experimentation fund (€6–8m).** Released by the governance forum on a rolling basis in tranches (Stage 1 ≤€25k, Stage 2 ≤€150k, Stage 3 into the normal capital process). Money committed once a year against forecast plans is the most common structural innovation killer in established companies.
- **Intercompany mechanics settled before the first cross-border experiment.** Agree with Group Tax a standing cost-sharing convention for multi-entity experiments — central bearing of Stage 1 and 2 costs, with benefit allocation on adoption. Transfer-pricing and cost-allocation friction terminates more cross-border collaboration than culture does.

---

## 9. Designing Voice for Different Contexts

Frameworks (Hofstede's power-distance and uncertainty-avoidance dimensions; Meyer's Culture Map on confrontation and negative-feedback directness; GLOBE) are useful **only to generate hypotheses for the diagnostic**, never as design inputs at country level. Within-country variance exceeds between-country variance often enough that designing from national averages produces confident errors. Design from what each site's diagnostic actually shows.

What is well-supported and travels: psychological safety predicts voice and learning behaviour (Edmondson); intrinsic motivation and autonomy support predict creative output (Amabile). The following claims from our earlier draft are downgraded to hypotheses for the diagnostic to test: that speed of permission outweighs volume of funding, and that voluntary teams outperform assigned ones on ambiguous problems.

**Mechanisms:**
- **Written and asynchronous first.** Ideas submitted in writing, in one's own language, in advance; then discussed. This equalises across language fluency, seniority, and comfort with public disagreement far more than any live brainstorm.
- **Funded language capacity.** Machine translation embedded in the platform, plus paid multilingual triage capacity at each hub (~€0.3m of the €0.8m platform line). A programme that diagnoses language as a barrier and funds nothing has diagnosed nothing.

## Fostering Innovation Across Borders: A Working Draft

### First, a gentle reframe

Before designing the intervention, it may be worth sitting with a question: *is the uneven innovation across locations a problem to be corrected, or a piece of information you haven't finished reading yet?*

The branches that appear less proactive are rarely populated by less creative people. More often, they've drawn accurate conclusions about what actually gets rewarded there — who gets promoted, whose ideas get quietly absorbed by a manager's own initiative, what happened to the last person who tried something and it didn't land. Innovation output is often a fairly honest mirror of local incentive structures and local memory.

So the most useful early move might be less "roll out an innovation program" and more "find out what each site already knows that we don't." A single global program imposed uniformly tends to produce compliance — decks, submitted ideas, participation metrics — while leaving the underlying conditions untouched.

With that in mind, here's what tends to work.

---

## 1. Create room, not requirements

**Protected time with no deliverable attached.** Whether it's 10% time, quarterly "exploration weeks," or simply a standing block that no one is allowed to book over — the essential design feature is that nothing is owed at the end. The moment exploration time requires a report, it becomes work with extra steps, and people will optimize for the report.

**Small, discretionary budgets held at low levels.** A few thousand euros/dollars that a team lead — or ideally an individual contributor — can spend on a prototype, a dataset, a tool, or a customer conversation without a business case. The amount matters less than the absence of an approval chain. Speed of permission is more predictive of innovation than volume of funding.

**Decision rights pushed down and made explicit.** Publish, in plain language, what people can decide alone. Ambiguity in authority defaults to caution: when someone can't tell whether they need permission, they assume they do, and the idea dies unspoken.

---

## 2. Make the cost of a failed attempt genuinely low

Risk-taking is a rational calculation, not a personality trait. People take risks when the downside is survivable and legible.

- **Reframe unit of accountability from "outcome" to "quality of the bet."** Was the hypothesis clear? Was the cost of learning proportionate? Was it stopped promptly when the evidence turned? A well-run experiment with a negative result is a success in every respect that matters.
- **Leaders narrate their own misses.** Not polished "failure celebrations" — those often read as theater, and in several cultural contexts as faintly humiliating. Something quieter works better: a senior person mentioning, in an ordinary meeting, the initiative they backed that went nowhere and what it taught them. Repeated, unremarkable, without drama.
- **Set explicit "reversible vs. irreversible" thresholds.** Reversible decisions get made fast and locally. Irreversible ones get scrutiny. Most organizations apply irreversible-decision governance to reversible decisions, and that is usually the whole problem.
- **Guarantee the landing.** Someone who spends nine months on an experiment that fails should have a clear, non-punitive path back — ideally a better one, since they now hold hard-won knowledge. If people watch a colleague's career stall after an honest attempt, no amount of messaging will undo it.

---

## 3. Design for the fact that "speaking up" means different things in different places

This is where uniform programs most often break. An open brainstorming session where junior people are expected to challenge senior colleagues in a second language, in real time, will surface ideas in some offices and near-silence in others — and the silence will be misread as an absence of ideas.

Some approaches that travel better:

- **Asynchronous and written first.** Ideas submitted in writing, in advance, ideally in one's own language, then discussed. This equalizes across language fluency, extroversion, and comfort with public disagreement.
- **Anonymous or pseudonymous channels as an entry ramp.** Not as a permanent state, but as a way to establish that ideas can be judged on merit before people risk attaching their names.
- **Write-then-discuss meetings.** Everyone reads a short document in silence and annotates before anyone speaks. Reduces the advantage of whoever is loudest or most senior.
- **Small-group and one-to-one formats** alongside plenary ones. Some of your best thinking will only ever surface in a conversation of three.
- **Distinguish "critique the idea" from "critique the person."** Explicit norms and framing here do real work in contexts where disagreement carries relational weight.

A test worth running: in offices that seem quiet, do ideas exist but stay unvoiced, or are they genuinely not being formed? Those are entirely different problems with entirely different remedies, and it's worth knowing which one you have before treating it.

---

## 4. Rebalance the centre–periphery relationship

Branches often behave passively because experience has taught them that headquarters decides, and that locally-originated ideas require more energy to defend than they're worth.

- **Reverse-flow expectation.** Make it normal — and visible — that products, processes, and practices originate outside HQ and get adopted centrally. One well-publicized instance of "this came from Kuala Lumpur and we're now rolling it out globally" is worth more than a year of encouragement.
- **Distribute mandates, not just tasks.** Give specific branches genuine ownership of a domain, product line, or customer segment where they hold real advantage. Ownership generates initiative; execution of someone else's plan generates competence.
- **Local market proximity as an asset, not noise.** The branches closest to fast-moving or resource-constrained markets are frequently your best source of frugal, unconventional solutions. Treat their divergence from central standards as a signal rather than a compliance issue.
- **Rotation and exchange.** Short placements, cross-border project pairs, and hosting arrangements. People carry norms in their bodies more reliably than in documents; a person who has worked in a high-initiative environment for three months brings something back that no training module conveys.

---

## 5. Build connective tissue between people, not between org boxes

Most genuinely novel ideas are recombinations — someone in one place learning what someone in another place already solved.

- **Internal talent/interest directories** so people can find each other by what they're curious about rather than by reporting line.
- **Communities of practice that cross geography and function,** with light facilitation and a modest budget, and no obligation to report upward.
- **"Working in the open" as default.** Visible work-in-progress, open documents, open channels. Serendipity requires visibility; it cannot be scheduled.
- **Fluid, merit-based team formation** for exploratory work — people opt in to problems that interest them rather than being assigned. Voluntary teams work harder on ambiguous problems than conscripted ones.
- **Cross-border pairing on experiments,** which quietly transfers norms and builds the trust that later makes candour possible.

---

## 6. Adjust the middle layer, or the rest won't hold

Middle management is where innovation initiatives most commonly go to die — not from malice, but because managers are still measured on predictability, utilization, and short-cycle delivery. Asking them to encourage experimentation while grading them on variance suppression is asking them to accept a personal cost.

- **Change what managers are evaluated on.** Include things like: number of experiments enabled, ideas from their team advanced beyond their own remit, people developed, decisions delegated. Make sponsoring someone else's idea a visible credit.
- **Give them cover.** A manager who backs a failed experiment needs to be seen being supported by their own leadership, publicly.
- **Reduce their permission-granting burden.** Every approval they don't need to give is one less bottleneck and one less implicit signal that ideas require sanction.
- **Coach the specific skill of receiving an unpolished idea.** The reflexive first response — "have you considered the cost?" — is often the exact moment innovation stops. Learning to ask "what would you need to test this cheaply?" instead is a small, teachable, high-leverage change.

---

## 7. Route ideas without bureaucratizing them

Idea pipelines tend to fail in one of two directions: no route at all, or a route so heavy it deters use.

A lighter architecture:

- **Very low submission threshold.** A short written form, in any language, no business case required.
- **A committed response time.** Anything submitted receives a substantive human reply within, say, two weeks. Nothing kills a suggestion scheme faster than silence — the second wave of ideas never comes.
- **Staged, small funding.** Tiny amounts to test cheaply; more only when evidence warrants. Optionality over commitment.
- **Idea authors stay attached** to their idea as it develops, with real involvement rather than a thank-you and a handover.
- **Visible graveyard.** Publish what was tried and stopped, and why. This normalizes stopping, prevents duplicated effort, and — importantly — demonstrates that the pipeline is real rather than decorative.

---

## 8. Recognition, handled carefully

Recognition is culturally loaded, and getting it wrong can be worse than doing nothing.

- **Offer forms of recognition and let people choose.** Individual spotlights land well in some contexts and cause acute discomfort in others. Team-level recognition, quiet advancement, additional autonomy, conference budgets, or time to pursue a next idea may each be the most valued reward depending on where and who.
- **The most powerful reward is usually more freedom.** Someone who ran a good experiment should get a bigger sandbox next time. This is legible everywhere.
- **Watch the promotion track closely.** If the people who advance are consistently reliable executors rather than productive experimenters, everyone will notice, and the stated culture will be correctly ignored.

---

## 9. Sequencing — a possible path

**Diagnose (first 6–8 weeks).** Not a survey asking "are you innovative?" Rather: What happened to the last three ideas you had? How long does approval take? What do you believe happens to someone here who tries something and it fails? Run this per-site and compare — the variance in the answers is your actual map.

**Pilot in willing sites (next 3–6 months).** Start where energy already exists — high-initiative branches and volunteer teams elsewhere. Voluntary participation gives you an honest read on whether the mechanisms work, uncontaminated by compliance. Resist the urge to be equitable about this too early; even coverage at low intensity produces less learning than deep pilots.

**Adapt, then extend (6–18 months).** Let each site tune the mechanics to local conditions while holding the outcomes constant. Uniformity of intent, variety of implementation. Recruit and equip local champions rather than deploying central programme managers.

**Institutionalize what proved itself.** By this point the changes worth keeping should be in the decision-rights documentation, the budget structure, and the promotion criteria — not in a communications campaign.

---

## What to keep an eye on

Watch behaviour, not sentiment:

- Time from idea to first cheap test
- Number of experiments started *and stopped* — the second number matters as much as the first
- Proportion of adopted initiatives originating outside HQ
- Number of decisions made without escalation
- Whether people who ran failed experiments are still advancing
- Whether second-time and third-time contributors exist, or only first-timers — repeat participation is the truest signal that the system is trusted

And a soft one worth attending to: are people bringing you *half-formed* ideas? A pipeline receiving only polished, defensible proposals is a pipeline in which people still feel they must pre-justify themselves.

---

## The uncomfortable part

Most of this is cheap and technically simple. The binding constraint is rarely the mechanism; it's whether the organization is genuinely willing to absorb the consequences of what it says it wants.

Some of what emerges will be inconvenient. Some will cannibalize existing revenue. Some will come from people whose judgment the centre hasn't previously trusted. Some will be visibly, expensively wrong.

The organization's response to the first genuinely awkward idea — and the first well-run experiment that fails publicly — will teach everyone more about the real culture than any programme ever could. Worth deciding in advance how you intend to handle that moment, because it will arrive sooner than expected, and everyone will be watching.

---

### A few questions worth sitting with

- Which of your locations is *already* innovating in ways the centre hasn't noticed — and what would it take to find out?
- If a promising idea appeared today in your quietest branch, how many people would need to say yes before anything happened? And how many of those yeses genuinely add information?
- What is the largest amount someone three levels down can spend without asking? What does that number communicate?
- Whose career here was visibly helped by an idea that didn't work?

The answers may make the priorities clearer than any framework could.

There is nothing on market sensing (customer feedback loops, competitive intelligence, front-line signal capture from the branches closest to the market), nothing on shortening the decision cycle for a *response*, and nothing on how a good idea in Kuala Lumpur becomes a shipped change in eight weeks. Responsiveness is a latency problem as much as a creativity problem, and latency is never addressed except obliquely via decision rights.

**2. No link to strategy.** There is no mechanism ensuring the ideas generated are the ideas the company needs. A low-threshold, no-business-case pipeline with staged funding will produce a large volume of unrelated micro-experiments. Missing: a small set of stated strategic challenge areas ("how do we serve SMEs in low-ARPU markets profitably?") that focus effort without dictating solutions. Missing: any portfolio framing (core / adjacent / new), any allocation logic, any explicit kill criteria beyond "visible graveyard."

**3. No prioritization.** Nine sections and roughly 45 discrete recommendations, all presented at equal weight. A client leadership team cannot act on this. What are the three moves for the first 90 days? Which two things, if done alone, deliver most of the benefit? My own read: (a) decision-rights publication plus reversible/irreversible thresholds, (b) manager scorecard change, (c) mandate distribution to two named branches. The other 42 items are downstream. The document should say so.

**4. Highest-leverage lever is buried.** "Rebalance the centre–periphery relationship" appears fourth, as bullets. For a multinational whose stated problem is *variance by location*, redistributing real mandates is likely the single most powerful intervention — it changes the structural incentive rather than the atmosphere. It deserves to lead, and it deserves specificity: which domains, to which sites, on what criteria, with what P&L and headcount consequences.

---

### B. Feasibility and execution gaps

**5. No cost, no resourcing, no trade-off acknowledgment.** "10% time" across a global workforce is a 10% payroll reallocation — an enormous, quantifiable cost that is never named, never sized, and never traded off against delivery commitments. It is also worth noting that 10% time has a mixed empirical track record (Google effectively wound it down; it tends to survive only where slack already exists and managers are rewarded for protecting it). Recommending it uncritically, and specifically the "nothing is owed at the end" variant, is the weakest recommendation in the document.

**6. No owner, no governance, no gates.** The sequencing section gives durations but no accountable executive, no steering mechanism, no decision criteria at each gate, no budget envelope, and no answer to "who does the work." A three-phase plan with no owner is a wish.

**7. The annual budget cycle is the elephant in the room.** For an established company, the most common structural innovation killer is that money is committed once a year against forecast plans. Without a ring-fenced, off-cycle experimentation fund with its own release rules, "staged, small funding" cannot function. Same applies to procurement and legal cycle times for prototype tooling and vendor sign-up — routinely 6–12 weeks, which destroys any cheap-test ambition.

**8. Currency parity error.** "A few thousand euros/dollars" of discretionary spend means radically different things in Zurich, São Paulo, and Manila — in relative authority, in what it buys, and in what it signals. Set it as a percentage of team cost base or PPP-adjust it. As written, it re-creates the centre–periphery inequality the document elsewhere tries to dissolve.

**9. Cross-border experiments have accounting friction.** Intercompany cost allocation and transfer pricing make multi-country volunteer teams administratively painful in many groups — one entity absorbs cost, another books benefit. This kills more cross-border collaboration than culture does. Not mentioned.

---

### C. The international dimension is thinner than the brief requires

This is the core of the request and it receives one section, largely about meeting formats.

**10. No framework, no evidence, and some soft stereotyping.** "In several cultural contexts as faintly humiliating" — which ones, and on what basis? Either engage a defensible model (power distance and uncertainty avoidance; Meyer's Culture Map on confrontation and negative-feedback directness; GLOBE) or drop the claim. Present-day best practice would also caution against country-level generalization as a design input beyond hypothesis generation.

**11. Legal and industrial-relations reality is entirely absent** — a serious omission for a multi-country programme:
- **Works councils / employee representation** (Germany, Netherlands, France, Nordics): changing manager evaluation criteria, reward schemes, working-time allocation, or introducing monitoring/participation metrics is frequently subject to consultation or co-determination. Timelines lengthen materially.
- **Employee invention compensation statutes** — Germany's *ArbnErfG*, Japan's Patent Act Art. 35, and others — create mandatory remuneration obligations for employee inventions. An idea pipeline that generates patentable output without addressing this creates real liability and inconsistent treatment across sites.
- **Anonymous channels and GDPR/works-council rules**, plus whistleblowing-directive overlap where anonymous submissions surface conduct issues rather than ideas.
- **"Guarantee the landing"** is straightforward under strong employment protection and considerably harder in at-will jurisdictions — worth naming rather than assuming uniform feasibility.
- **Language** is diagnosed correctly but funded nowhere: no machine translation in the platform, no multilingual triage capacity, no budget line.

---

### D. Internal contradictions left unresolved

**12. The pilot logic conflicts with the stated problem.** The client's problem is *variance between locations*. The recommendation is to pilot where energy already exists and "resist the urge to be equitable." That optimizes for learning speed while predictably widening the gap in the near term — and it leaves the quiet branches receiving attention last, reinforcing exactly the centre-periphery message the document warns about. This may still be the right call, but it must be argued explicitly with a parallel low-cost intervention for the lagging sites (e.g., decision-rights publication and manager coaching everywhere from day one, deep pilots only where willing).

**13. Anonymity vs. attachment vs. recognition.** §3 recommends anonymous channels as an entry ramp; §7 requires idea authors to stay attached to their ideas; §8 builds recognition around contribution. These three cannot all be true at once. Also unaddressed: anonymous channels commonly degrade into low-quality suggestion boxes with no follow-up loop, and in low-trust environments they can entrench the belief that attribution is dangerous rather than dissolve it.

**14. Gameable metrics after warning about gameable metrics.** The document rightly attacks "participation metrics" as compliance theatre, then proposes "number of experiments enabled" as a manager KPI — a textbook gameable count. Either pair it with a quality gate (peer or portfolio review of bet quality) or use it as a diagnostic indicator, explicitly not a scored target.

---

### E. Rigor issues

**15. Assertions presented as findings.** "Speed of permission is more predictive of innovation than volume of funding." "Voluntary teams work harder on ambiguous problems than conscripted ones." Both are plausible; neither is sourced. Either cite (Amabile on intrinsic motivation and creativity; Edmondson on psychological safety; Birkinshaw on subsidiary initiative — which is directly on point for the centre-periphery argument) or mark them as hypotheses to test in the diagnostic.

**16. False dichotomy in measurement.** "Watch behaviour, not sentiment" overcorrects. Validated psychological-safety instruments give you a comparable cross-site baseline that behavioural metrics take a year to produce — provided you adjust for well-documented cross-cultural response bias (acquiescence, extreme-response, and modesty effects) and read the *within-site trend* rather than the between-site absolute. Discarding sentiment measurement entirely removes your only early leading indicator.

**17. No baseline, no targets, no business outcome.** The metrics list is behaviourally intelligent but unquantified and disconnected from results. Add: revenue or margin from offerings launched in the last 24–36 months, time-to-market on competitive responses, share of that revenue originating outside HQ. Without an outcome tier, this programme is unfundable at the second budget review.

---

### F. Form and tone

**18. Register is wrong for the audience.** "A gentle reframe," "a working draft," "questions worth sitting with," "the uncomfortable part." This is coaching-essay voice. Combined with pervasive hedging — "it may be worth," "a possible path," "tends to work," "some approaches that travel better" — the document reads as under-committed. A client paying for expertise needs a recommendation, with the confidence interval stated once rather than reasserted in every paragraph.

**19. No executive summary and no one-page view.** Add a front-page summary: the diagnosis in three lines, the three priority moves, cost envelope, expected outcomes, and the two biggest risks. Add a summary table mapping intervention → owner → cost → time-to-effect → primary metric.

**20. Redundancy — roughly 25% compressible.** Decision rights appear in §1, again as reversible/irreversible in §2, again as "reduce permission burden" in §6, and again in the closing questions. Recognition is split across §2 ("guarantee the landing"), §6 ("visible credit"), and §8.

**21. Closing questions are misplaced.** They are good questions — better than most of the recommendations, in fact — but arriving after the answers, they undercut the deliverable. Move them to the front as the diagnostic instrument, or convert them into a formal per-site diagnostic protocol with the four questions already drafted in §9.

---

### Required revisions

1. Add an executive summary with three prioritized moves for the first 90 days and a cost envelope.
2. Add a market-responsiveness workstream: signal capture, decision latency targets, and a route from front-line insight to shipped change.
3. Add strategic focus areas and a portfolio/kill logic so idea volume converts to strategic value.
4. Add the legal/IR layer: works-council consultation, employee-invention remuneration, data protection, and the country-level sequencing consequences.
5. Resolve the three contradictions (pilot-selection vs. variance reduction; anonymity vs. attribution; gameable manager metrics).
6. Name an accountable executive, governance forum, gate criteria, and budget — including a ring-fenced off-cycle experimentation fund.
7. Replace or heavily qualify the 10% time recommendation; size its cost if retained.
8. PPP-adjust or percentage-base the discretionary spend authority.
9. Add a baseline-and-target measurement tier including business outcomes; restore a bounded, bias-adjusted use of sentiment data.
10. Cut hedging, cut ~25% of length, and move the diagnostic questions to the front.

# Building Innovation Capacity Across a Multinational Footprint
### Recommendation to the Executive Committee — for review with country leadership before release

**Stated assumptions** (to be corrected in week 1, before anything is announced): ~6,000–10,000 employees; 12–18 countries; established core business; group revenue in the €1.5–2.5bn range. All figures below scale with these numbers. Confidence in the structural recommendations (Moves 1–3, funding mechanics, legal sequencing) is high; confidence in site-level design choices is deliberately low until the diagnostic is complete, and those choices are left to local leadership.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

**Diagnosis.** The variance between locations is not a variance in creative capability; it is a variance in local mandate, decision latency, and remembered consequence. Branches with no real domain ownership, long approval chains, and a visible example of an unrewarded attempt behave exactly as rational people should. Middle management is the binding layer: managers are currently measured on predictability while being asked to sponsor variance.

**The three moves for the first 90 days** (everything else in this paper is downstream of these):

| # | Move | Why first |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Transfer two genuine domain mandates to two named branches**, with P&L and headcount attached | Changes structural incentive, not atmosphere. Highest leverage on location variance. |
| **2** | **Publish group-wide decision rights and reversible/irreversible thresholds**, with a decision-latency clock | The only intervention that reaches every site at once and closes the equity gap created by piloting. |
| **3** | **Change the manager scorecard** (with an anti-gaming quality gate), beginning works-council consultation in week 1 | Without this, Moves 1 and 2 are absorbed and neutralised at the middle layer. |

**Year-1 cost envelope: €9–14m**, of which €6–8m is a ring-fenced off-cycle experimentation fund (recoverable as portfolio investment, not overhead), €2.2m sized slack time in designated roles, €0.8m platform and translation capacity, €0.4m diagnostic, and ~€1.5m rotation and exchange.

**Expected outcomes by month 24:** competitive-response time-to-market reduced from baseline (to be measured; typically 24–30 weeks in companies of this profile) to ≤10 weeks; idea-to-first-cheap-test from ~90 days to ≤21 days; share of newly adopted group initiatives originating outside HQ rising from baseline to ≥35%.

**The two biggest risks.** (i) *Relational risk:* mandate transfer and manager re-scoring will be read at HQ and by some country heads as a loss of standing. If this is announced before individual pre-alignment with each affected leader, resistance will be quiet, indefinite, and very difficult to name. (ii) *Structural risk:* the annual budget cycle. If experimentation money is not ring-fenced off-cycle, staged funding cannot function and the programme dies at the second budget review.

---

## 2. Summary Table

| Intervention | Accountable owner | Year-1 cost | Time to effect | Primary metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mandate transfer to 2 branches | COO (Exec Sponsor: CEO) | Cost-neutral (reallocation) | 6–12 months | Share of adopted initiatives originating outside HQ |
| Decision rights + reversible/irreversible thresholds | Group General Counsel + COO | <€0.2m | 60–90 days | % decisions closed without escalation; approval-step count |
| Manager scorecard change | CHRO | <€0.3m (+ consultation time) | 6–9 months (IR-dependent) | Bet-quality review score; ideas advanced beyond manager's remit |
| Ring-fenced experimentation fund | CFO | €6–8m | 90 days to open | Idea-to-first-test days; portfolio kill rate |
| Market-signal capture and latency clock | Chief Strategy / Commercial Officer | €0.5m | 3–6 months | Signal-to-decision days |
| Sized slack (designated roles only) | Site heads | €2.2m | 6 months | Experiments started *and* stopped |
| Voice design + language capacity | CHRO + site heads | €0.8m | 3–9 months | Repeat contributor ratio; within-site safety trend |
| Rotation and cross-border pairing | CHRO | €1.5m | 12–18 months | Cross-site initiatives; norm transfer (qualitative) |
| Legal/IR enablement (invention remuneration, GDPR, councils) | GC + CHRO | €0.4m | Prerequisite | Countries cleared to launch |

---

## 3. Diagnostic First — The Instrument (Weeks 1–6)

Run this per site, through the site's own leadership rather than around it, and in the local language. Local leaders should see their site's results before the centre discusses them; this preserves standing and produces honest data.

Four questions to each of ~15 people per site, plus documented process trace:

1. **What happened to the last three ideas you had?** (Trace each: raised / absorbed / declined / never voiced — and to whom.)
2. **How many people must say yes before something small can be tried, and how long does that take in calendar days?** (Verify against actual records.)
3. **What do people here believe happens to someone who tries something and it does not work?** (Ask about "people here," not the respondent — this reduces exposure and yields better data in higher power-distance and higher uncertainty-avoidance settings.)
4. **Whose career here was visibly helped by an idea that did not work?** (Name or blank. A blank answer is the finding.)

Plus: which locations are *already* innovating in ways the centre has not noticed? Ask customers and country finance, not only management.

The variance in the answers is the actual map. Two hypotheses must be separated before treating anything: **ideas exist but stay unvoiced** (a safety and channel problem) versus **ideas are not being formed** (a mandate and market-exposure problem). These require different remedies.

---

## 4. Move 1 — Redistribute Real Mandates (Lead Lever)

Subsidiary initiative rises with the substance of local charter, not with encouragement (Birkinshaw's work on subsidiary initiative is directly on point; we treat this as well-supported).

**Selection criteria for the first two mandates:**
- Genuine local advantage: proximity to a fast-moving, price-sensitive, or regulation-leading market
- Existing initiative signal from the diagnostic (a site already improvising)
- A customer segment or product line where central standards are demonstrably a poor fit
- Site leadership willing to accept accountability, confirmed privately in advance

**What "mandate" must include, or it will not be believed:** P&L ownership for the domain; headcount authority; product roadmap authority for that domain including the right to diverge from group standards with documented reasoning; a seat at the group product forum; and a defined multi-year horizon so the site is not judged on quarter three.

**Reverse flow, made visible.** When a practice originating in a non-HQ site is adopted group-wide, the announcement names the originating site and its people. One such adoption is worth more than a year of messaging. Handle the mirror case with care: adopting from a branch should never be framed as HQ having been wrong, which costs face at the centre and slows the second adoption.

**Pre-alignment is not optional.** Before any announcement: individual conversations with the HQ function heads who will lose scope, with the two receiving site heads, and with the country heads not selected — including a stated pathway for the next round. Consensus built quietly in advance is what makes the public step uncontroversial.

---

## 5. Move 2 — Decision Rights, Thresholds, and Latency (One Consolidated Change)

This is the universal floor: it goes to every site on day one, including — especially — the quiet ones.

- **Publish, in plain language and every working language, what each level can decide alone.** Ambiguity in authority defaults to caution: where people cannot tell whether permission is needed, they assume it is.
- **Classify decisions reversible vs. irreversible.** Reversible: decided locally, fast, no committee. Irreversible or reputation-bearing: full scrutiny and senior involvement. Most established companies apply irreversible-decision governance to reversible decisions; that single misclassification explains much of the observed inertia.
- **Cap approval steps** for reversible spend below threshold at one.
- **Set a decision-latency target and measure it**: signal-to-decision ≤10 working days for reversible market responses; funded experiment start ≤21 days from submission.
- **Discretionary spend authority set as a percentage, not a currency figure.** Recommendation: a team lead may commit up to **2% of their team's annual cost base per quarter** without a business case, floored at a locally meaningful minimum and reviewed against local PPP. A flat "few thousand euros" grants a Zurich lead trivial latitude and a Manila lead unusual latitude — and re-creates the centre–periphery inequality we are trying to dissolve.
- **Procurement and legal fast lane.** A pre-approved vendor list, standard short-form contract, and 5-working-day SLA for experiment-scale purchases below threshold. Standard cycles of 6–12 weeks make "cheap test" impossible regardless of culture.

---

## 6. Move 3 — The Middle Layer

Asking managers to sponsor variance while grading them on variance suppression asks them to accept a personal cost. Correct the scorecard, and protect their standing while doing it.

**Add to manager evaluation (weighted ~15–20%):**
- **Bet quality, peer-reviewed** — not experiment count. A quarterly portfolio review by a small cross-site panel scores the manager's supported experiments on hypothesis clarity, proportionality of cost, and promptness of stopping. This replaces the gameable count; raw counts are retained as a diagnostic indicator only, explicitly unscored.
- **Ideas advanced beyond the manager's own remit** — sponsoring someone else's idea into another unit earns visible credit.
- **Decisions delegated** and permission requests eliminated.

**Cover, given publicly and specifically.** A manager who backs a well-run experiment that fails must be seen being supported by their own superior, in the same forum where the failure became visible. This is the single cheapest and most decisive signal available.

**One teachable skill, coached at scale.** The reflexive first response to an unpolished idea — "have you considered the cost?" — is the moment innovation usually stops. The substitute: "what would you need to test this cheaply?" Small, teachable, high-leverage.

**Consultation before announcement.** In Germany, the Netherlands, France, Austria and the Nordics, changes to evaluation criteria, reward schemes, working-time allocation, and any participation monitoring frequently fall under works-council consultation or co-determination. Begin in week 1. Treated as a partnership, councils shorten adoption; treated as an obstacle, they extend it by two or three quarters. Sequence country launches accordingly and do not pretend to a uniform go-live date.

---

## 7. Market Responsiveness — The Latency Workstream

Creativity and responsiveness are different problems. Responsiveness is latency.

- **Front-line signal capture.** Every customer-facing role gets a 60-second structured channel for one thing: "what I heard that we cannot currently serve." Local language, mobile, no form. Weekly triage at site level, not at HQ.
- **Named signal owners per market.** One accountable person per country compiles a monthly two-page market delta: competitor moves, regulatory shifts, lost-deal reasons, and price signals. Sites nearest fast-moving markets are treated as sensors, not as noise.
- **A single latency clock, published.** Signal received → decision → shipped change. Publish the median and the worst case monthly by region. Visibility of the clock does more than any exhortation.
- **A standing weekly response forum** with pre-delegated authority to commit up to a defined threshold. Decisions in the forum, not after it.
- **Divergence from central standards read as signal.** Where a site has quietly worked around a group process to serve its market, the default question is what the workaround reveals, not who authorised it.

Target state: front-line insight in Kuala Lumpur to shipped change in eight weeks for reversible product or pricing responses, with the site deciding, not requesting.

---

## 8. Strategic Focus and Portfolio Logic

Without focus, a low-threshold pipeline produces high volume and low strategic value.

- **Four to six named strategic challenge questions**, set by the Executive Committee, refreshed annually, phrased as problems not solutions — e.g. "how do we serve SMEs profitably in low-ARPU markets?"; "where does regulation in Market X become an advantage?" Ideas outside these areas remain welcome but are funded from a smaller pool.
- **Portfolio allocation:** 70% core improvement / 20% adjacent / 10% new-to-company, allocated at group level and reviewed quarterly. Sites hold their own sub-portfolios.
- **Explicit kill criteria set at funding, not at review.** Every funded experiment states in advance what result would stop it and by when. Stopping on pre-agreed criteria is recorded as successful execution — this removes the personal cost of stopping and protects the sponsor's standing.
- **Ring-fenced, off-cycle experimentation fund (€6–8m).** Released by the governance forum on a rolling basis in tranches (Stage 1 ≤€25k, Stage 2 ≤€150k, Stage 3 into the normal capital process). Money committed once a year against forecast plans is the most common structural innovation killer in established companies.
- **Intercompany mechanics settled before the first cross-border experiment.** Agree with Group Tax a standing cost-sharing convention for multi-entity experiments — central bearing of Stage 1 and 2 costs, with benefit allocation on adoption. Transfer-pricing and cost-allocation friction terminates more cross-border collaboration than culture does.

---

## 9. Designing Voice for Different Contexts

Frameworks (Hofstede's power-distance and uncertainty-avoidance dimensions; Meyer's Culture Map on confrontation and negative-feedback directness; GLOBE) are useful **only to generate hypotheses for the diagnostic**, never as design inputs at country level. Within-country variance exceeds between-country variance often enough that designing from national averages produces confident errors. Design from what each site's diagnostic actually shows.

What is well-supported and travels: psychological safety predicts voice and learning behaviour (Edmondson); intrinsic motivation and autonomy support predict creative output (Amabile). The following claims from our earlier draft are downgraded to hypotheses for the diagnostic to test: that speed of permission outweighs volume of funding, and that voluntary teams outperform assigned ones on ambiguous problems.

**Mechanisms:**
- **Written and asynchronous first.** Ideas submitted in writing, in one's own language, in advance; then discussed. This equalises across language fluency, seniority, and comfort with public disagreement far more than any live brainstorm.
- **Funded language capacity.** Machine translation embedded in the platform, plus paid multilingual triage capacity at each hub (~€0.3m of the €0.8m platform line). A programme that diagnoses language as a barrier and funds nothing has diagnosed nothing.
- **Write-then-discuss meetings.** Silent reading and annotation before anyone speaks.
- **Small-group and one-to-one channels** alongside plenary ones, and a standing route through a respected senior figure for people who prefer to raise matters through relationship rather than platform. Ideas that arrive this way count fully.
- **Norms distinguishing critique of the idea from critique of the person**, stated explicitly, because in many settings the two are hard to separate in public.

**Attribution — resolving the anonymity contradiction.** A three-stage ladder, chosen by the contributor, not by the company:

1. **Confidential intake** (identity known only to a named local intake owner, not to the contributor's line manager). This is the default entry route. Fully anonymous submission is *not* offered: it produces no follow-up loop, degrades into a suggestion box, invites whistleblowing-directive and GDPR complications when submissions concern conduct rather than ideas, and entrenches the belief that attribution is dangerous.
2. **Named on progression.** When an idea is funded at Stage 1, the contributor is invited — not required — to attach their name and stay involved. Involvement is the norm; opting out is permitted and recorded without comment.
3. **Recognition by consent.** Nothing is publicised without the contributor's explicit choice of form.

**Recognition, offered as a menu.** Individual spotlights land well in some settings and cause acute discomfort in others. Offer team-level recognition, quiet advancement, additional autonomy, conference or study budget, or protected time for a next idea — and let people choose. The most universally legible reward is a larger sandbox next time.

**Consequence management, protecting face.** People who ran honest, well-designed experiments that failed must be visibly still advancing. Where employment protection is strong, a guaranteed return path is straightforward; in at-will jurisdictions it must be written into the programme charter as an explicit commitment, or it will not be credible. Learning is shared through *documented cases* and a published register of what was stopped and why — the facts, not a person on a stage. Senior leaders reference their own unsuccessful bets quietly and in ordinary meetings; staged "failure celebrations" read as theatre in most contexts and as humiliation in several.

---

## 10. Slack Time — Sized and Bounded

We do not recommend group-wide 10% time. Across 8,000 people it is a ~€60m annual payroll reallocation, it has a mixed empirical record (including at the company most associated with it), and it survives only where slack already exists and managers are rewarded for protecting it — which is not yet true here.

**Recommended instead:** 4% protected time (roughly one afternoon a fortnight) for ~600 designated roles in engineering, product, service design, and front-line commercial teams in participating sites. Cost ≈ **€2.2m**. Protected in the calendar by the site head, not the line manager. A one-paragraph note of what was explored is expected quarterly — not a report, not a business case, not a deliverable. Extend only where the manager scorecard change has already taken effect.

---

## 11. Governance, Sequencing, and the Equity Question

**Accountable executive:** the **COO**, with the **CEO as Executive Sponsor**. Programme direction sits with a **Group Innovation Council**: COO (chair), CFO, CHRO, Chief Strategy/Commercial Officer, General Counsel, and three rotating country heads — with at least two from non-HQ regions at all times. Meets monthly; decisions by consensus of the Council with the COO holding the casting decision where consensus is not reached, so that a single objection cannot stall the port
